analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $5.25 an hour in yearly steps.
analysis.headline: The minimum wage bill died in a House subcommittee in 1995 without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in steps from $4.25 an hour to $5.25 an hour over about four years. It was introduced by a House Democrat in January 1995, sent to the House labor committee, and referred to a subcommittee. No hearing, vote, or further action ever happened, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The millions of workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage would see their hourly pay rise in steps from $4.25 to $5.25 over roughly four years [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers earning near the minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from the existing $4.25 an hour to $4.50, then $4.75, then $5.00, then $5.25 in yearly steps, directly increasing pay for workers at the bottom of the wage scale.
Phases the increase in over roughly four years rather than all at once, giving employers time to adjust to each step.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum wage — restaurants, retail stores, hotels, and other low-wage businesses — would bear the higher payroll costs, and some of that cost would likely be passed to customers through higher prices [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Businesses that employ many minimum-wage workers would bear higher payroll costs, and opponents of wage floors argue some entry-level jobs or hours could be reduced as employers adjust.
The first step of the bill, $4.25 an hour, simply maintained the minimum wage at its existing level for six months, so the real increase did not begin until a year after enactment.
The bill contained no indexing to inflation, so the value of the $5.25 floor would have eroded over time absent future legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: a higher wage floor raises pay for low-wage workers and shifts costs onto minimum-wage employers and, in part, their customers. The staged four-year phase-in reduces the shock to employers, but the bill was blunt — a single national figure with no regional cost-of-living adjustment and no inflation indexing, so the real value of $5.25 would have drifted down over time. Its larger weakness was political: it never received the hearing or debate that could have tested and refined the design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to a House subcommittee in February 1995 and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it simply sat there until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on January 31, 1995 and referred to the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities.
On February 17, 1995 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill died when the 104th Congress ended without ever reaching a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of low-wage workers — restaurants, retail, and other minimum-wage businesses — were better off because the bill never advanced and no higher wage floor was imposed. Low-wage workers gained nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers who avoided a mandated raise

for.name: Rep. Albert Russell Wynn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.role: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities (Republican-led)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never brought it to a markup or a floor vote; it died in the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the seven sponsors and cosponsors were all Democrats, and the Republican-run committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have raised their wage floor to $5.25 an hour, directly increasing payroll costs. Its death in subcommittee meant no increase came from this bill.
Large low-wage employers would have faced the same higher payroll costs. The bill never advanced, so no cost was imposed.
